Clinical Vignette: Layla

Layla sits in the office with her hands folded carefully in her lap, her posture precise and controlled. At sixty-three, she maintains the professional bearing of someone who has spent four decades in financial auditing—meticulous, organized, present. Yet there is a brittleness to her composure that becomes apparent as she speaks about the last three years of her life.

Her younger brother Karim was killed in a car accident. He was struck by a drunk driver while crossing the street near his home in Los Angeles, where he lived with his wife and two children. Layla was in her apartment in San Francisco when she received the call from her sister-in-law. She remembers every detail with crystalline clarity: the time of day, the exact words spoken, the sound of traffic in the background, the way her legs seemed to stop working beneath her.

She had been close to Karim. They had immigrated together as young adults, navigated the complexities of building new lives in a country that often felt foreign. He had looked to her for guidance; she had protected him. The guilt of not being able to protect him from that moment—from a senseless intersection on a Tuesday afternoon—has become a permanent weight she carries.

In the months following his death, Layla's life contracted significantly. She took a leave of absence from her position as a senior auditor at a mid-sized firm, a decision that felt necessary at the time but has now become three years long. She cannot seem to return. When she sits at her desk at home, attempting to review financial statements, the numbers blur together. Her mind fractures into fragments: images of Karim's face, the hospital waiting room, the funeral, her nephew asking when Uncle Karim was coming home.

Sleep has become a negotiation between her body and her mind. She lies awake for hours, her thoughts looping through scenarios where she rewrites history—where she had called Karim that morning, where he had stayed home, where the drunk driver had taken a different route. When sleep finally comes, it brings nightmares. She dreams of the accident repeatedly, though she never witnessed it. In her dreams, she is always there, always unable to reach him in time.

The hypervigilance has infiltrated her daily life in unexpected ways. When she drives, she grips the steering wheel so tightly her hands ache. Every car that approaches from a side street triggers a spike of panic. She finds herself catastrophizing—imagining accidents, sudden deaths, disasters that might befall the people she loves. She has become overly cautious with her remaining family, calling her sister too frequently, worrying excessively about her niece and nephew.

What troubles Layla most is the emotional numbness that has settled alongside the anxiety. She attends family gatherings but feels disconnected, as if observing herself from outside her body. Food tastes like nothing. She has lost interest in the small pleasures that once structured her days—her morning coffee, her weekly phone call with her cousin, the satisfaction of a completed audit. The world has become a place where terrible, random things happen, and she is powerless to prevent them.

She has avoided returning to work, convinced that she cannot concentrate, that she would make mistakes, that she is no longer capable of the precise attention her profession demands. Her colleagues have stopped calling. Her identity as a competent, reliable woman—the auditor, the older sister, the problem-solver—has become something she can no longer recognize in the mirror.
